title: Network Interfaces, MAC Addresses, Ethernet Frames & ARP Neighbor Cache
topic: MAC Addresses, Ethernet Frames, ARP, Broadcast vs. Unicast, Switching
learning_objectives: Inspect active host network interfaces and differentiate real Ethernet MAC addresses from loopback.
Explain how ARP maps an IPv4 address to a Layer 2 MAC address using broadcast requests and unicast replies.
Understand why Layer 2 Ethernet/ARP visibility depends on the physical or virtual capture interface.

concept_explanation.title: Ethernet Frames & 48-Bit MAC Addresses
concept_explanation.summary: On local Ethernet/Wi-Fi links, Layer 2 frames carry 48-bit source and destination MAC addresses plus an EtherType field (0x0800 for IPv4, 0x0806 for ARP).
key_points: Unicast frames target a single NIC's MAC address; broadcast frames target ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
Layer 2 switches learn which MAC address lives on each switch port by reading source MAC headers.

concept_explanation.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
concept_explanation.summary: Before sending an IPv4 packet on a LAN segment, a host must know the next-hop MAC address. ARP broadcasts 'Who has IP X?' and caches the unicast reply.
key_points: ARP operates strictly within a single Layer 2 broadcast domain (it does not cross routers).
Resolved entries appear in the OS neighbor/ARP cache (ip neigh) as REACHABLE or STALE.

experiment.title: Inspect Real Host Interfaces, MAC Addresses & ARP Neighbor Cache
experiment.instructions: Run a safe, read-only Layer 2 inspection of this host's interfaces (`ip -j link`) and real OS neighbor/ARP table (`ip -j neigh`). If non-loopback traffic is present, NetBox honestly reports what is directly observable without fabricating Ethernet or ARP frames.
required_setup: Optional: non-loopback interface with active LAN/gateway traffic
execution_steps: Click Run Experiment to inspect live host link-layer interfaces and ARP/neighbor entries.
Compare the loopback (`lo`) interface (00:00:00:00:00:00) against `eth0` (real MAC address and MTU 1500).
Inspect the real OS neighbor table entries (gateway IPv4 -> MAC address mappings).

supported_scenarios.label: Inspect Live Interfaces & ARP Neighbor Table
supported_scenarios.description: Reads actual Linux link-layer addresses, broadcast addresses, MTUs, and OS ARP/neighbor cache entries.

expected_observations: Loopback interface `lo` reports zeroed MAC address (00:00:00:00:00:00) and large loopback MTU (65536).
Ethernet/virtual interface `eth0` reports a real 48-bit MAC address, broadcast ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, and MTU 1500.
OS neighbor cache shows real IPv4-to-MAC mappings (e.g., default gateway) if recent traffic occurred.
observation_caveats: Loopback (127.0.0.1) traffic never traverses physical Ethernet and has no real ARP exchange.
In WSL 2 NAT environments, `eth0` connects to the Hyper-V virtual switch rather than raw Wi-Fi frames; NetBox reports only genuine observed entries and never fabricates ARP packets.

questions.prompt: Why is an ARP Request sent to destination MAC address ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff?
options: To route the packet across the Internet to a public DNS server.
Because the sender does not yet know the target's MAC address, so it must broadcast the query to all nodes on the local L2 segment.
Because Ethernet frames cannot carry unicast IPv4 addresses.
To encrypt the payload before transmitting over Wi-Fi.
questions.rubric_summary: Broadcast destination MAC ensures all hosts on the LAN segment receive the ARP query.
questions.explanation: An ARP Request uses Layer 2 broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) so every device on the local broadcast domain inspects the target IP and the owner replies with its unicast MAC.

questions.prompt: Host A (192.168.1.10/24) sends an IPv4 packet to a remote server 8.8.8.8 via default gateway 192.168.1.1. Whose MAC address goes in the Ethernet destination MAC field leaving Host A?
options: The MAC address of the default gateway (192.168.1.1)
questions.rubric_summary: Destination IP stays 8.8.8.8, while destination MAC is the local next-hop router (default gateway).
questions.explanation: Layer 2 MAC addresses only carry frames across a single hop. For off-subnet destinations, the Ethernet destination MAC is the default gateway's MAC address while IP destination stays 8.8.8.8.

questions.prompt: Why does capturing traffic on Linux loopback (`lo`) show zeroed MAC addresses and no ARP packets?
questions.rubric_summary: Loopback stays inside the host kernel without an Ethernet LAN or next-hop MAC resolution.
questions.explanation: Loopback traffic never leaves the host kernel onto an Ethernet medium, so no ARP resolution or physical NIC MAC addressing takes place.

completion_criteria.description: Run the Layer 2 interface/ARP inspection and score at least 67% on the assessment.
